resources.title: Explaining Black Box Predictions and Unveiling Data Artifacts through Influence Functions
resources.abstract: Modern deep learning models for NLP are notoriously opaque.This has motivated the development of methods for interpreting such models, e.g., via gradient-based saliency maps or the visualization of attention weights.Such approaches aim to provide explanations for a particular model prediction by highlighting important words in the corresponding input text.While this might be useful for tasks where decisions are explicitly influenced by individual tokens in the input, we suspect that such highlighting is not always suitable for tasks where model decisions should be driven by more complex reasoning.In this work, we investigate the use of influence functions for NLP, providing an alternative approach to interpreting neural text classifiers.Influence functions explain the decisions of a model by identifying influential training examples.Despite the promise of this approach, influence functions have not yet been extensively evaluated in the context of NLP, a gap addressed by this work.We conduct a comparison between influence functions and common word-saliency methods on representative tasks.As suspected, we find that influence functions are particularly useful for natural language inference, a task in which 'saliency maps' may not provide clear interpretation.Furthermore, we develop a new quantitative measure based on influence functions that can reveal artifacts in training data.

No training record among the ten most influential for any audited declined application is a known data-entry or labelling error

For each false positive in the spam filter's audit sample, the ten most influential training emails were reviewed and the cause of the error, mislabelled or unrepresentative training data, was recorded
The training records most influential for the audited protected-group rejections were reviewed, and none comes from underwriting rules since withdrawn or from branches with a documented bias

techniques.name: Contrastive Explanation Method
techniques.description: The Contrastive Explanation Method (CEM) explains one prediction of a classifier, such as a neural network, by describing what is present and what is absent in the input. A pertinent positive is the smallest set of features already present that is enough for the model to give the same prediction. A pertinent negative is the smallest set of features not currently present that would change the prediction to a different class if they were added. CEM finds both by solving an optimisation problem that searches for the smallest change to the input, and it can use an autoencoder (a model trained to reconstruct realistic inputs) to keep the changed inputs realistic. An explanation reads like 'this digit is a 3 because these strokes are present and because a short bar at the top is absent', since adding that bar would make it a 5.

example_use_cases.description: A procurement team uses a neural-network model that rates invoices as low, medium or high risk. For a high-risk invoice, the pertinent positives are the few triggered events that are enough for that rating, such as a large amount and a vendor with only a PO box. The pertinent negatives are events that did not occur but would lower the rating if they had, such as the vendor being registered. Reviewers check both before blocking payment.

A clinician reviews a decision-support model that suggests flu rather than pneumonia for a patient. The pertinent positives are the findings that are enough for that suggestion, such as cough, cold and fever. The pertinent negatives are findings that are absent but would move the suggestion to pneumonia if present, such as sputum and chills. The clinician compares both with their own reasoning to judge whether the model weighs the right findings.

A council uses a model to screen applications for housing support. When an application is declined, the pertinent negatives show which missing items, such as proof of tenancy, would have changed the outcome if present. A caseworker checks that each item is something the applicant can provide, then includes it in the decision notice.

limitations.description: Each explanation needs its own optimisation run for a single instance, so explaining many decisions is slow. Models whose gradients cannot be accessed need numerical gradient estimates, which slows it further.

Several settings shape the result, including how strongly the search favours small changes, how confident the model must be in the new class, and whether an autoencoder is used. Different settings can give different pertinent positives and negatives for the same instance, so they need checking with someone who knows the domain.

Changed inputs can be unrealistic. Without an autoencoder trained on good-quality data, a pertinent negative may describe an input that could never occur, so the explanation says little about real cases. Where data is scarce or poor, a good autoencoder may not be possible.

Absence has to be defined by the user. CEM adds or removes features relative to a value that stands for no signal, such as a blank pixel, and a poor choice gives meaningless pertinent negatives. This is natural for images and binary indicators, and needs domain judgement for continuous or categorical tabular data.

A pertinent negative is the smallest change the model responds to, not advice a person can act on. It may involve a feature that cannot be changed, such as age, and nothing in the method checks that the change is feasible. It is most useful when the two classes are close; if they are very different, there can be too many pertinent negatives to read.

resources.title: Explanations based on the Missing: Towards Contrastive Explanations with Pertinent Negatives
resources.abstract: In this paper we propose a novel method that provides contrastive explanations justifying the classification of an input by a black box classifier such as a deep neural network. Given an input we find what should be %necessarily and minimally and sufficiently present (viz. important object pixels in an image) to justify its classification and analogously what should be minimally and necessarily \emph{absent} (viz. certain background pixels). We argue that such explanations are natural for humans and are used commonly in domains such as health care and criminology. What is minimally but critically \emph{absent} is an important part of an explanation, which to the best of our knowledge, has not been explicitly identified by current explanation methods that explain predictions of neural networks. We validate our approach on three real datasets obtained from diverse domains; namely, a handwritten digits dataset MNIST, a large procurement fraud dataset and a brain activity strength dataset. In all three cases, we witness the power of our approach in generating precise explanations that are also easy for human experts to understand and evaluate.

resources.title: Contrastive Explanations Method (CEM) applied to MNIST — Alibi Explain
Understanding How CNNs Recognize Facial Expressions: A Case Study with LIME and CEM
resources.abstract: Recognizing facial expressions has been a persistent goal in the scientific community. Since the rise of artificial intelligence, convolutional neural networks (CNN) have become popular to recognize facial expressions, as images can be directly used as input. Current CNN models can achieve high recognition rates, but they give no clue about their reasoning process. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) has been developed as a means to help to interpret the results obtained by machine learning models. When dealing with images, one of the most-used XAI techniques is LIME. LIME highlights the areas of the image that contribute to a classification. As an alternative to LIME, the CEM method appeared, providing explanations in a way that is natural for human classification: besides highlighting what is sufficient to justify a classification, it also identifies what should be absent to maintain it and to distinguish it from another classification. This study presents the results of comparing LIME and CEM applied over complex images such as facial expression images. While CEM could be used to explain the results on images described with a reduced number of features, LIME would be the method of choice when dealing with images described with a huge number of features.

sample_claims.text: For the invoices the risk model rates high, compliance reviewers judge that the pertinent positives are sufficient grounds for the rating and the pertinent negatives are events that would lower it.
For each flagged patient record, the pertinent positives and negatives match the findings clinicians use to tell the model's diagnosis from the nearest alternative.
On the instances tested, keeping only the pertinent positive leaves the model's prediction unchanged, and adding the pertinent negative changes it to a different class.
Each applicant declined for credit is told which absent factors, if present, would have changed the model's decision, and a reviewer has confirmed that each is something the applicant could change.
Caseworkers can tell an applicant which missing information, if provided, would change the eligibility model's outcome for that application.

techniques.name: Monte Carlo Dropout
techniques.description: Monte Carlo dropout estimates how uncertain a neural network is about each prediction. Dropout randomly switches off some of the network's units and is normally used only in training, but here it stays on at prediction time. Each forward pass (one run of an input through the network) therefore uses a different random pattern of units, and the input is run through typically tens to a hundred times. The average gives the prediction, and the spread across runs is read as epistemic uncertainty, meaning uncertainty from the model's limited knowledge rather than noise in the data. The method approximates Bayesian inference, but the spread is an estimate whose reliability should be checked against held-out errors.

example_use_cases.description: Quantifying diagnostic uncertainty in medical imaging models by running 50+ Monte Carlo forward passes to detect when a chest X-ray classification is highly uncertain, prompting radiologist review for borderline cases.

An autonomous-driving team replays recorded camera footage through its object detector with dropout left on, and finds the scenes (night rain, unusual vehicles) where detections vary most between passes. It uses them to decide what data to collect and which scenarios to add to simulation testing.

A grid operator's demand-forecasting network, trained with dropout, is run 100 times each morning. Days on which the forecasts spread beyond the planners' tolerance are sent for human review before reserve capacity is booked.

limitations.description: The spread across passes reflects uncertainty about the model's parameters, not noise in the data that varies from input to input. An input in a very noisy region can still show a narrow spread, so a narrow spread does not mean the outcome is predictable.

Each prediction needs many forward passes, typically 50 to 100, so inference costs that many times more compute, and too few passes make the spread itself unstable. The passes can run in parallel, which limits added delay but not total compute, so real-time or edge deployments with tight budgets may not afford it.

The network must have been trained with dropout, and the derivation assumes it sits before every weight layer. A model trained without dropout has to be retrained, so the technique is often unavailable for models already built or bought in.

The size of the spread depends on the dropout probability and weight decay, which the developer sets or tunes on validation data rather than learns from the data. The uncertainty scale is partly a design choice and needs checking against held-out errors.

The spread is an approximation, and its behaviour depends on the architecture. In the original paper's regression experiments, uncertainty kept growing away from the training data with ReLU activations but stayed bounded with TanH, so a narrow spread on unfamiliar inputs is not proof of familiarity.

resources.title: Dropout as a Bayesian Approximation: Representing Model Uncertainty in Deep Learning
resources.abstract: Deep learning tools have gained tremendous attention in applied machine learning. However such tools for regression and classification do not capture model uncertainty. In comparison, Bayesian models offer a mathematically grounded framework to reason about model uncertainty, but usually come with a prohibitive computational cost. In this paper we develop a new theoretical framework casting dropout training in deep neural networks (NNs) as approximate Bayesian inference in deep Gaussian processes. A direct result of this theory gives us tools to model uncertainty with dropout NNs -- extracting information from existing models that has been thrown away so far. This mitigates the problem of representing uncertainty in deep learning without sacrificing either computational complexity or test accuracy. We perform an extensive study of the properties of dropout's uncertainty. Various network architectures and non-linearities are assessed on tasks of regression and classification, using MNIST as an example. We show a considerable improvement in predictive log-likelihood and RMSE compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, and finish by using dropout's uncertainty in deep reinforcement learning.

resources.title: Training a LeNet with Monte Carlo dropout - TorchUncertainty Docs
Leveraging uncertainty information from deep neural networks for disease detection
resources.abstract: Deep learning (DL) has revolutionized the field of computer vision and image processing. In medical imaging, algorithmic solutions based on DL have been shown to achieve high performance on tasks that previously required medical experts. However, DL-based solutions for disease detection have been proposed without methods to quantify and control their uncertainty in a decision. In contrast, a physician knows whether she is uncertain about a case and will consult more experienced colleagues if needed. Here we evaluate drop-out based Bayesian uncertainty measures for DL in diagnosing diabetic retinopathy (DR) from fundus images and show that it captures uncertainty better than straightforward alternatives. Furthermore, we show that uncertainty informed decision referral can improve diagnostic performance. Experiments across different networks, tasks and datasets show robust generalization. Depending on network capacity and task/dataset difficulty, we surpass 85% sensitivity and 80% specificity as recommended by the NHS when referring 0−20% of the most uncertain decisions for further inspection. We analyse causes of uncertainty by relating intuitions from 2D visualizations to the high-dimensional image space. While uncertainty is sensitive to clinically relevant cases, sensitivity to unfamiliar data samples is task dependent, but can be rendered more robust.

techniques.name: Permutation Tests
techniques.description: A permutation test asks how likely an observed result would be if there were no real relationship in the data. The tester shuffles the data many times in a way that breaks the relationship under test, recalculates the metric each time, and takes the p-value as the share of shuffled results at least as extreme as the real one. Shuffling the outcome labels and retraining tests whether a classifier's accuracy beats chance, and shuffling group membership tests whether a gap between groups in the rate of decisions, such as approvals, is larger than chance would produce. A restricted variant, Ojala and Garriga's second test, shuffles each feature's values separately within each class, which keeps every feature's own spread but breaks the relationships between features, so a classifier that makes significantly fewer errors on the real data than on the shuffled copies is using those relationships. The test needs no assumption about the shape of the data's distribution, but a small p-value does not show that an effect is large, important or causal.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital research group trains a classifier on 80 patients with thousands of gene-expression measurements. With so few cases, a good cross-validated accuracy could be luck, so it repeats the whole training and testing procedure on thousands of label-shuffled copies and reports the result only if it beats nearly all of them.

A council analytics team replacing a case-prioritisation model checks whether the new model's higher accuracy on the same test cases could be chance. It randomly swaps the two models' predictions case by case 10,000 times, recomputes the gap each time, and switches only if the real gap is larger than nearly all of the shuffled ones.

A bank's model-risk team sees a higher approval rate for one applicant group than another in a loan model's decisions. Before escalating, it shuffles group membership across applicants thousands of times and recomputes the gap, to test whether a gap this large could arise by chance. A significant gap prompts a fuller review but does not by itself show unlawful discrimination.

A cardiology team using a gradient-boosted model to flag high blood pressure expects height and weight to matter together, not only alone. It shuffles each feature within each outcome class 1,000 times and tests at the 5% level whether the model errs less on the real data, to decide if a simpler model treating features separately would do. A non-significant result means either the features are unrelated within classes or the model ignores the relationship.

limitations.description: Each permutation needs the metric recalculated, and a model may need retraining every time, so thousands of permutations of a large model can be expensive. Stricter thresholds need more permutations, because the smallest possible p-value is 1 divided by the number of permutations plus one, and repeated runs can disagree near the threshold.

Assumes exchangeability of observations under the null hypothesis, which may be violated in time series or hierarchical data structures, where simple shuffling gives p-values that are too small or too large.

A significant result shows that the data are unlikely under the stated null, such as 'features and labels are independent'. It does not show that the effect is large, important or causal, and shuffling cannot rule out a confounder or an artefact of how the data were collected.

Testing many features or groups at once produces some false positives by chance, so the p-values need correcting, for example with a false discovery rate procedure. Without that, a feature-by-feature test over many features will flag some that are only noise.

What is shuffled defines the question answered. Shuffling labels tests whether features and labels are related at all, while shuffling features within classes tests whether a classifier uses dependencies between features. The wrong scheme answers a different question from the one the assurance claim needs.

Permutation Tests for Studying Classifier Performance
resources.abstract: We explore the framework of permutation-based p-values for assessing the behavior of the classification error. In this paper we study two simple permutation tests. The first test estimates the null distribution by permuting the labels in the data; this has been used extensively in classification problems in computational biology. The second test produces permutations of the features within classes, inspired by restricted randomization techniques traditionally used in statistics. We study the properties of these tests and present an extensive empirical evaluation on real and synthetic data. Our analysis shows that studying the classification error via permutation tests is effective; in particular, the restricted permutation test clearly reveals whether the classifier exploits the interdependency between the features in the data.

resources.title: Nonparametric permutation tests for functional neuroimaging: A primer with examples
resources.abstract: Requiring only minimal assumptions for validity, nonparametric permutation testing provides a flexible and intuitive methodology for the statistical analysis of data from functional neuroimaging experiments, at some computational expense. Introduced into the functional neuroimaging literature by Holmes et al. ([ 1996 ]: J Cereb Blood Flow Metab 16:7–22), the permutation approach readily accounts for the multiple comparisons problem implicit in the standard voxel‐by‐voxel hypothesis testing framework. When the appropriate assumptions hold, the nonparametric permutation approach gives results similar to those obtained from a comparable Statistical Parametric Mapping approach using a general linear model with multiple comparisons corrections derived from random field theory. For analyses with low degrees of freedom, such as single subject PET/SPECT experiments or multi‐subject PET/SPECT or f MRI designs assessed for population effects, the nonparametric approach employing a locally pooled (smoothed) variance estimate can outperform the comparable Statistical Parametric Mapping approach. Thus, these nonparametric techniques can be used to verify the validity of less computationally expensive parametric approaches. Although the theory and relative advantages of permutation approaches have been discussed by various authors, there has been no accessible explication of the method, and no freely distributed software implementing it. Consequently, there have been few practical applications of the technique. This article, and the accompanying MATLAB software, attempts to address these issues. The standard nonparametric randomization and permutation testing ideas are developed at an accessible level, using practical examples from functional neuroimaging, and the extensions for multiple comparisons described. Three worked examples from PET and f MRI are presented, with discussion, and comparisons with standard parametric approaches made where appropriate. Practical considerations are given throughout, and relevant statistical concepts are expounded in appendices.

techniques.name: Demographic Parity Assessment
techniques.description: Demographic Parity Assessment checks whether a model gives a favourable outcome, such as a loan approval or an interview invitation, to each demographic group at the same rate. It compares those rates without adjusting for how many people in each group would qualify. Statistical Parity Difference is the gap between group rates (a signed difference between two named groups in AIF360, the highest rate minus the lowest across all groups in Fairlearn), and the Disparate Impact ratio divides the lowest rate by the highest. A ratio below 0.8 is a common warning sign, following the four-fifths rule used by US employment regulators. A gap shows that outcomes differ between groups but not why, and equal rates do not show that individuals were treated fairly.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's model risk team compares loan approval rates for applicants of different ethnic groups in the validation sample before a credit model goes live. It reports the ratio of the lowest to the highest approval rate and checks it against the 0.8 rule of thumb from US employment practice, treating a lower ratio as a prompt to investigate rather than a verdict.

An employer's HR analytics team tracks each month the share of male and female applicants that a CV-screening tool passes to interview. A widening gap in pass rates triggers a review of the tool before the next hiring round, even where the two applicant pools differ.

A local council checks whether its automated screening tool refers benefit claims for fraud investigation at similar rates across ethnic groups. Because a referral is a burden rather than a benefit, a higher referral rate for one group is a red flag that officers then examine case by case.

limitations.description: Parity can be met by unfair selection. A model can match approval rates by choosing less suitable applicants from one group, and the metric looks only at outcome rates, so it cannot tell. Dwork et al. give this as a standard example of why parity alone is not enough.

May penalise a model for real differences between groups in how many members qualify (the base rate), such as differing clinical need by age, and so push towards artificial equality where none should exist.
Can conflict with individual fairness principles, where similarly qualified individuals might receive different treatment to achieve group parity.

A pass on one attribute can hide large gaps inside subgroups, such as older women within a comparison by gender. The common 0.8 ratio threshold is a rule of thumb from US employment practice, so passing it is a screen rather than evidence of compliance in other domains.
A rate ratio depends on which group is the reference and can be unstable when its positive rate is very small. It is undefined when the denominator rate is zero.

resources.title: Fairness Through Awareness
resources.abstract: We study fairness in classification, where individuals are classified, e.g., admitted to a university, and the goal is to prevent discrimination against individuals based on their membership in some group, while maintaining utility for the classifier (the university). The main conceptual contribution of this paper is a framework for fair classification comprising (1) a (hypothetical) task-specific metric for determining the degree to which individuals are similar with respect to the classification task at hand; (2) an algorithm for maximizing utility subject to the fairness constraint, that similar individuals are treated similarly. We also present an adaptation of our approach to achieve the complementary goal of "fair affirmative action," which guarantees statistical parity (i.e., the demographics of the set of individuals receiving any classification are the same as the demographics of the underlying population), while treating similar individuals as similarly as possible. Finally, we discuss the relationship of fairness to privacy: when fairness implies privacy, and how tools developed in the context of differential privacy may be applied to fairness.

resources.title: Certifying and Removing Disparate Impact
resources.abstract: What does it mean for an algorithm to be biased? In U.S. law, unintentional bias is encoded via disparate impact, which occurs when a selection process has widely different outcomes for different groups, even as it appears to be neutral. This legal determination hinges on a definition of a protected class (ethnicity, gender) and an explicit description of the process. When computers are involved, determining disparate impact (and hence bias) is harder. It might not be possible to disclose the process. In addition, even if the process is open, it might be hard to elucidate in a legal setting how the algorithm makes its decisions. Instead of requiring access to the process, we propose making inferences based on the data it uses. We present four contributions. First, we link disparate impact to a measure of classification accuracy that while known, has received relatively little attention. Second, we propose a test for disparate impact based on how well the protected class can be predicted from the other attributes. Third, we describe methods by which data might be made unbiased. Finally, we present empirical evidence supporting the effectiveness of our test for disparate impact and our approach for both masking bias and preserving relevant information in the data. Interestingly, our approach resembles some actual selection practices that have recently received legal scrutiny.

resources.title: A Data-Centric Approach to Detecting and Mitigating Demographic Bias in Pediatric Mental Health Text: A Case Study in Anxiety Detection
resources.abstract: Introduction: Healthcare AI models often inherit biases from their training data. While efforts have primarily targeted bias in structured data, mental health heavily depends on unstructured data. This study aims to detect and mitigate linguistic differences related to non-biological differences in the training data of AI models designed to assist in pediatric mental health screening. Our objectives are: (1) to assess the presence of bias by evaluating outcome parity across sex subgroups, (2) to identify bias sources through textual distribution analysis, and (3) to develop a de-biasing method for mental health text data. Methods: We examined classification parity across demographic groups and assessed how gendered language influences model predictions. A data-centric de-biasing method was applied, focusing on neutralizing biased terms while retaining salient clinical information. This methodology was tested on a model for automatic anxiety detection in pediatric patients. Results: Our findings revealed a systematic under-diagnosis of female adolescent patients, with a 4% lower accuracy and a 9% higher False Negative Rate (FNR) compared to male patients, likely due to disparities in information density and linguistic differences in patient notes. Notes for male patients were on average 500 words longer, and linguistic similarity metrics indicated distinct word distributions between genders. Implementing our de-biasing approach reduced diagnostic bias by up to 27%, demonstrating its effectiveness in enhancing equity across demographic groups. Discussion: We developed a data-centric de-biasing framework to address gender-based content disparities within clinical text. By neutralizing biased language and enhancing focus on clinically essential information, our approach demonstrates an effective strategy for mitigating bias in AI healthcare models trained on text.

resources.title: An empirical characterization of fair machine learning for clinical risk prediction
resources.abstract: The use of machine learning to guide clinical decision making has the potential to worsen existing health disparities. Several recent works frame the problem as that of algorithmic fairness, a framework that has attracted considerable attention and criticism. However, the appropriateness of this framework is unclear due to both ethical as well as technical considerations, the latter of which include trade-offs between measures of fairness and model performance that are not well-understood for predictive models of clinical outcomes. To inform the ongoing debate, we conduct an empirical study to characterize the impact of penalizing group fairness violations on an array of measures of model performance and group fairness. We repeat the analysis across multiple observational healthcare databases, clinical outcomes, and sensitive attributes. We find that procedures that penalize differences between the distributions of predictions across groups induce nearly-universal degradation of multiple performance metrics within groups. On examining the secondary impact of these procedures, we observe heterogeneity of the effect of these procedures on measures of fairness in calibration and ranking across experimental conditions. Beyond the reported trade-offs, we emphasize that analyses of algorithmic fairness in healthcare lack the contextual grounding and causal awareness necessary to reason about the mechanisms that lead to health disparities, as well as about the potential of algorithmic fairness methods to counteract those mechanisms. In light of these limitations, we encourage researchers building predictive models for clinical use to step outside the algorithmic fairness frame and engage critically with the broader sociotechnical context surrounding the use of machine learning in healthcare.

sample_claims.text: The recruitment system's job offer rates are statistically equivalent across gender groups
The automated lending platform produces approval decisions at equal rates for all ethnic demographics
The medical referral system assigns specialist appointments at consistent rates across patient age groups
The benefits allocation system provides positive outcomes at equal rates across protected demographic categories
The admissions algorithm produces acceptance decisions at statistically indistinguishable rates for applicants from different socioeconomic backgrounds

techniques.name: Adversarial Debiasing
techniques.description: Adversarial debiasing trains a model so that its predictions carry as little information as possible about a protected attribute, such as sex or race. Two neural networks are trained together, a predictor that learns the main task, such as estimating default risk, and an adversary that tries to guess each person's protected attribute from the predictor's output. The predictor is updated to stay accurate while making the adversary's guesses fail, which pushes its outputs towards equal rates of favourable outcomes across groups (demographic parity). If the adversary is also given the true label, the predictor is penalised only for information about the attribute beyond what the label carries, which targets equal error rates across groups (equalised odds). The method needs the protected attribute for every training example and a model trained by gradient descent.

example_use_cases.description: A technology company trains a CV-screening model with an adversary that tries to guess each applicant's gender from the model's shortlisting score, so that selection rates come out similar for men and women (demographic parity) instead of leaning on CV features that happen to correlate with gender.

A lender trains a default-risk model for loan approvals with an adversary that is given each applicant's score and true repayment outcome and tries to guess their age band, so that false-positive and false-negative rates are similar across age bands (equalised odds) while predictive accuracy is kept.

A hospital group trains a COVID-19 screening model on emergency-department data with an adversary that tries to guess patient ethnicity from the model's score and the true test result, so that error rates are similar across ethnic groups while screening performance stays clinically useful.

limitations.description: The adversary only sees what it is given, usually the predictor's score and, for equalised odds, the true label. The method therefore targets one output-level criterion and gives no assurance that hidden layers are free of protected-attribute information, or that a different criterion holds.
Needs the protected attribute for every training example, so it cannot be used where that attribute was never collected or may not be held.

Demographic parity and equalised odds generally cannot both be met, so one must be chosen before training. Equal error rates can also come from worsening one group's rates: in the original Adult income experiment, the false-positive rate for women rose from 0.025 to 0.065.

Training two networks against each other is unstable. The weight given to the adversary has to be tuned (adversary_loss_weight in AIF360), and a wrong setting can make training diverge or leave the result closer to a different criterion than the one intended.

The paper's guarantee that outputs meet the chosen criterion holds only if both networks converge and the adversary is strong enough. A weak adversary leaves bias in place, and the convexity assumptions behind the proof do not hold for typical neural networks, so fairness has to be checked on held-out data after training.

resources.title: On the Fairness ROAD: Robust Optimization for Adversarial Debiasing
resources.abstract: In the field of algorithmic fairness, significant attention has been put on group fairness criteria, such as Demographic Parity and Equalized Odds. Nevertheless, these objectives, measured as global averages, have raised concerns about persistent local disparities between sensitive groups. In this work, we address the problem of local fairness, which ensures that the predictor is unbiased not only in terms of expectations over the whole population, but also within any subregion of the feature space, unknown at training time. To enforce this objective, we introduce ROAD, a novel approach that leverages the Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO) framework within a fair adversarial learning objective, where an adversary tries to infer the sensitive attribute from the predictions. Using an instance-level re-weighting strategy, ROAD is designed to prioritize inputs that are likely to be locally unfair, i.e. where the adversary faces the least difficulty in reconstructing the sensitive attribute. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our method: it achieves Pareto dominance with respect to local fairness and accuracy for a given global fairness level across three standard datasets, and also enhances fairness generalization under distribution shift.

resources.title: Mitigating Unwanted Biases with Adversarial Learning
resources.abstract: Machine learning is a tool for building models that accurately represent input training data. When undesired biases concerning demographic groups are in the training data, well-trained models will reflect those biases. We present a framework for mitigating such biases by including a variable for the group of interest and simultaneously learning a predictor and an adversary. The input to the network X, here text or census data, produces a prediction Y, such as an analogy completion or income bracket, while the adversary tries to model a protected variable Z, here gender or zip code. The objective is to maximize the predictor's ability to predict Y while minimizing the adversary's ability to predict Z. Applied to analogy completion, this method results in accurate predictions that exhibit less evidence of stereotyping Z. When applied to a classification task using the UCI Adult (Census) Dataset, it results in a predictive model that does not lose much accuracy while achieving very close to equality of odds (Hardt, et al., 2016). The method is flexible and applicable to multiple definitions of fairness as well as a wide range of gradient-based learning models, including both regression and classification tasks.

resources.title: An adversarial training framework for mitigating algorithmic biases in clinical machine learning
resources.abstract: Machine learning is becoming increasingly prominent in healthcare. Although its benefits are clear, growing attention is being given to how these tools may exacerbate existing biases and disparities. In this study, we introduce an adversarial training framework that is capable of mitigating biases that may have been acquired through data collection. We demonstrate this proposed framework on the real-world task of rapidly predicting COVID-19, and focus on mitigating site-specific (hospital) and demographic (ethnicity) biases. Using the statistical definition of equalized odds, we show that adversarial training improves outcome fairness, while still achieving clinically-effective screening performances (negative predictive values >0.98). We compare our method to previous benchmarks, and perform prospective and external validation across four independent hospital cohorts. Our method can be generalized to any outcomes, models, and definitions of fairness.

sample_claims.text: On held-out data, the shortlisting model's selection rates differ between gender groups by no more than the agreed tolerance, and its accuracy is within the agreed margin of the unconstrained model.
The default-risk model's false-positive and false-negative rates differ between age bands by no more than the agreed tolerance on held-out data.
The COVID-19 screening model's error rates are similar across ethnic groups in each external hospital cohort, with negative predictive value above the clinical threshold set for screening.
Compared with the same model trained without the adversary, the model's gap on the chosen fairness criterion is smaller on held-out data, at a reported cost in accuracy.

techniques.name: Causal Discrimination Testing
techniques.description: Causal discrimination testing checks whether a system gives different outputs to otherwise identical inputs because of a protected attribute, by changing only that attribute, or a name, term or other proxy that signals it, and measuring how often or how much the output changes. Galhotra, Brun and Meliou (2017), who called the approach fairness testing, generate inputs from a description of the valid input fields, make copies of each that differ only in the protected attribute (for example, recorded sex), run them all through the system as a black box, and report the causal discrimination score: the share of inputs whose decision changes, sampled until it is known within a chosen margin of error and confidence level. For text, the same test substitutes identity terms or names in otherwise unchanged sentences, such as one religion or ethnicity for another, and reports the average change in the model's score across the substitutions, which Garg et al. (2019) call the counterfactual token fairness gap. Because every other part of the input is held fixed, the test needs no model of how the attribute influences other variables: it measures whether the system itself responds to the attribute, or to the chosen proxy. The output is a score per attribute and, if the tester logs them, the input pairs whose outputs differed.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's model validation team tests a credit-approval model before release. For a sample of last year's applications it changes only the applicant's recorded sex, and separately their marital status, re-scores each pair, and reports the share of decisions that flip with a confidence interval, against a release threshold agreed with the compliance function.

A trust-and-safety team checks a toxicity classifier used to hold comments for review by substituting identity terms such as 'gay', 'Muslim' or 'Black' across a set of non-toxic comments. It measures the average change in toxicity score for each term and flags any term whose substitution pushes benign comments over the moderation threshold.

An HR technology supplier tests its CV-ranking service before a client deploys it, by submitting the same CVs under first names and surnames associated with different ethnicities and genders and reporting how often each candidate's rank or shortlisting changes.

A hospital's AI assurance lead tests a symptom-triage assistant with clinical vignettes that differ only in the patient's stated ethnicity. Clinicians first mark which vignettes should be unaffected by ethnicity, and only those pairs count as failures when the urgency rating changes.

limitations.description: Holding every other input fixed measures only the system's direct response to the attribute or proxy. It does not follow through the effects the attribute has on other inputs, such as career breaks on an employment history. Garg et al. note that token substitution is more limited than counterfactual fairness defined on a causal model. Where those downstream effects matter, a clean result does not show that individuals were treated fairly.

The test covers only what is perturbed. Unlisted identity terms, unperturbed proxies and multi-word references go undetected, as does discrimination that appears only when attributes change together: Galhotra et al. measured 11.2% for gender alone but 77.2% for gender, marital status and race together. Garg et al. found mitigation for listed terms generalised much less to held-out terms. A pass covers only the perturbations tried, and the list needs domain review.

Generated inputs may be unrealistic. Themis draws inputs uniformly from the input schema, so the score covers combinations that never occur in practice. Testing real inputs or an existing test suite avoids that, but the score is then only as representative as that set. Galhotra et al. note that Themis computes no confidence level for it, and an interval from a random sample of real cases covers sampling error only.

Not every substitution should leave the output unchanged. Garg et al. give 'That's so gay' versus 'That's so straight' as a pair a toxicity model may rightly score differently, and clinical risk can legitimately depend on sex. Without a judgement about which pairs must match, the test raises false alarms or, if such pairs are excluded wholesale, hides real failures.

A model can pass and still produce very different outcome or error rates across groups, because the test asks only whether changing the attribute changes the output, not whether outcomes are equal. Galhotra et al. distinguish this causal discrimination from group discrimination, and Garg et al. note that a text classifier can satisfy counterfactual fairness while completely failing equality of odds, so it does not replace group metrics.

resources.title: Themis: a software fairness tester (LASER-UMASS/Themis)
resources.abstract: Themis™ is a software fairness tester.

resources.title: Fairness testing: testing software for discrimination
resources.abstract: This paper defines software fairness and discrimination and develops a testing-based method for measuring if and how much software discriminates, focusing on causality in discriminatory behavior. Evidence of software discrimination has been found in modern software systems that recommend criminal sentences, grant access to financial products, and determine who is allowed to participate in promotions. Our approach, Themis, generates efficient test suites to measure discrimination. Given a schema describing valid system inputs, Themis generates discrimination tests automatically and does not require an oracle. We evaluate Themis on 20 software systems, 12 of which come from prior work with explicit focus on avoiding discrimination. We find that (1) Themis is effective at discovering software discrimination, (2) state-of-the-art techniques for removing discrimination from algorithms fail in many situations, at times discriminating against as much as 98% of an input subdomain, (3) Themis optimizations are effective at producing efficient test suites for measuring discrimination, and (4) Themis is more efficient on systems that exhibit more discrimination. We thus demonstrate that fairness testing is a critical aspect of the software development cycle in domains with possible discrimination and provide initial tools for measuring software discrimination.

resources.title: BiasFinder: Metamorphic Test Generation to Uncover Bias for Sentiment Analysis Systems
resources.abstract: Artificial intelligence systems, such as Sentiment Analysis (SA) systems, typically learn from large amounts of data that may reflect human bias. Consequently, such systems may exhibit unintended demographic bias against specific characteristics (e.g., gender, occupation, country-of-origin, etc.). Such bias manifests in an SA system when it predicts different sentiments for similar texts that differ only in the characteristic of individuals described. To automatically uncover bias in SA systems, this paper presents BiasFinder, an approach that can discover biased predictions in SA systems via metamorphic testing. A key feature of BiasFinder is the automatic curation of suitable templates from any given text inputs, using various Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques to identify words that describe demographic characteristics. Next, BiasFinder generates new texts from these templates by mutating words associated with a class of a characteristic (e.g., gender-specific words such as female names, she, her). These texts are then used to tease out bias in an SA system. BiasFinder identifies a bias-uncovering test case (BTC) when an SA system predicts different sentiments for texts that differ only in words associated with a different class (e.g., male vs. female) of a target characteristic (e.g., gender). We evaluate BiasFinder on 10 SA systems and 2 large scale datasets, and the results show that BiasFinder can create more BTCs than two popular baselines. We also conduct an annotation study and find that human annotators consistently think that test cases generated by BiasFinder are more fluent than the two baselines.

resources.title: Counterfactual Fairness in Text Classification through Robustness
resources.abstract: In this paper, we study counterfactual fairness in text classification, which asks the question: How would the prediction change if the sensitive attribute referenced in the example were different? Toxicity classifiers demonstrate a counterfactual fairness issue by predicting that "Some people are gay" is toxic while "Some people are straight" is nontoxic. We offer a metric, counterfactual token fairness (CTF), for measuring this particular form of fairness in text classifiers, and describe its relationship with group fairness. Further, we offer three approaches, blindness, counterfactual augmentation, and counterfactual logit pairing (CLP), for optimizing counterfactual token fairness during training, bridging the robustness and fairness literature. Empirically, we find that blindness and CLP address counterfactual token fairness. The methods do not harm classifier performance, and have varying tradeoffs with group fairness. These approaches, both for measurement and optimization, provide a new path forward for addressing fairness concerns in text classification.

resources.title: Gender, Race, and Intersectional Bias in Resume Screening via Language Model Retrieval
resources.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) hiring tools have revolutionized resume screening, and large language models (LLMs) have the potential to do the same. However, given the biases which are embedded within LLMs, it is unclear whether they can be used in this scenario without disadvantaging groups based on their protected attributes. In this work, we investigate the possibilities of using LLMs in a resume screening setting via a document retrieval framework that simulates job candidate selection. Using that framework, we then perform a resume audit study to determine whether a selection of Massive Text Embedding (MTE) models are biased in resume screening scenarios. We simulate this for nine occupations, using a collection of over 500 publicly available resumes and 500 job descriptions. We find that the MTEs are biased, significantly favoring White-associated names in 85.1% of cases and female-associated names in only 11.1% of cases, with a minority of cases showing no statistically significant differences. Further analyses show that Black males are disadvantaged in up to 100% of cases, replicating real-world patterns of bias in employment settings, and validate three hypotheses of intersectionality. We also find an impact of document length as well as the corpus frequency of names in the selection of resumes. These findings have implications for widely used AI tools that are automating employment, fairness, and tech policy.

techniques.name: Federated Learning
techniques.description: Federated learning trains one shared model across several parties, such as phones or hospitals, without collecting their data in one place. Each party trains the current model on its own data and sends back only an update, such as the changed weights (the model's internal numbers) or the gradients (the direction of change). A central coordinator combines the updates, typically by averaging, into an improved shared model and sends it out again, and the cycle repeats over many rounds. Raw records stay with their owners, which limits how much sensitive data is stored or moved and can support data protection rules that favour collecting less. It is not a privacy guarantee on its own, because updates can still reveal information about the data behind them and the coordinator has to be trusted.

example_use_cases.description: A mobile keyboard team trains a next-word prediction model on users' phones and receives only model updates, so typed text never reaches its servers. The team uses this to decide whether personalised suggestions can ship without collecting message content centrally.

Hospitals in several countries train a model that predicts COVID-19 outcomes on their own patient records and share only model updates with a coordinating centre, so no patient record leaves a hospital. Each hospital's data governance board uses this to decide whether it can join the collaboration.

Several banks jointly train a fraud-detection model on their own transaction data and share only model updates, so no bank's customer records reach a competitor. Each bank's compliance team uses the setup to decide whether joint training fits its data-sharing restrictions.

limitations.description: Communication overhead can be substantial, especially with frequent model updates and large models, potentially limiting scalability and increasing training time compared to centralised approaches.

Statistical heterogeneity across participants (non-IID data distributions) can lead to training instability, slower convergence, and reduced model performance compared to centralised training on pooled data.
System heterogeneity in computational capabilities, network connectivity, and availability of participating devices can create bottlenecks and introduce bias towards more capable participants.
Privacy vulnerabilities remain through gradient leakage attacks, model inversion, and membership inference attacks that can potentially reconstruct sensitive information from shared model updates.

A faulty or malicious participant can submit harmful updates that the coordinator cannot check against the participant's data, for example to plant a hidden backdoor in the shared model. Defences such as robust aggregation add cost, and the coordinator must also be trusted with the updates it receives.

resources.title: Communication-Efficient Learning of Deep Networks from Decentralized Data
resources.abstract: Modern mobile devices have access to a wealth of data suitable for learning models, which in turn can greatly improve the user experience on the device. For example, language models can improve speech recognition and text entry, and image models can automatically select good photos. However, this rich data is often privacy sensitive, large in quantity, or both, which may preclude logging to the data center and training there using conventional approaches. We advocate an alternative that leaves the training data distributed on the mobile devices, and learns a shared model by aggregating locally-computed updates. We term this decentralized approach Federated Learning. We present a practical method for the federated learning of deep networks based on iterative model averaging, and conduct an extensive empirical evaluation, considering five different model architectures and four datasets. These experiments demonstrate the approach is robust to the unbalanced and non-IID data distributions that are a defining characteristic of this setting. Communication costs are the principal constraint, and we show a reduction in required communication rounds by 10-100x as compared to synchronized stochastic gradient descent.

resources.title: Federated Learning - DeepLearning.AI
Federated learning for predicting clinical outcomes in patients with COVID-19
resources.abstract: Federated learning (FL) is a method used for training artificial intelligence models with data from multiple sources while maintaining data anonymity, thus removing many barriers to data sharing. Here we used data from 20 institutes across the globe to train a FL model, called EXAM (electronic medical record (EMR) chest X-ray AI model), that predicts the future oxygen requirements of symptomatic patients with COVID-19 using inputs of vital signs, laboratory data and chest X-rays. EXAM achieved an average area under the curve (AUC) >0.92 for predicting outcomes at 24 and 72 h from the time of initial presentation to the emergency room, and it provided 16% improvement in average AUC measured across all participating sites and an average increase in generalizability of 38% when compared with models trained at a single site using that site's data. For prediction of mechanical ventilation treatment or death at 24 h at the largest independent test site, EXAM achieved a sensitivity of 0.950 and specificity of 0.882. In this study, FL facilitated rapid data science collaboration without data exchange and generated a model that generalized across heterogeneous, unharmonized datasets for prediction of clinical outcomes in patients with COVID-19, setting the stage for the broader use of FL in healthcare.

resources.title: Federated learning enables big data for rare cancer boundary detection
resources.abstract: Although machine learning (ML) has shown promise across disciplines, out-of-sample generalizability is concerning. This is currently addressed by sharing multi-site data, but such centralization is challenging/infeasible to scale due to various limitations. Federated ML (FL) provides an alternative paradigm for accurate and generalizable ML, by only sharing numerical model updates. Here we present the largest FL study to-date, involving data from 71 sites across 6 continents, to generate an automatic tumor boundary detector for the rare disease of glioblastoma, reporting the largest such dataset in the literature ( n = 6, 314). We demonstrate a 33% delineation improvement for the surgically targetable tumor, and 23% for the complete tumor extent, over a publicly trained model. We anticipate our study to: 1) enable more healthcare studies informed by large diverse data, ensuring meaningful results for rare diseases and underrepresented populations, 2) facilitate further analyses for glioblastoma by releasing our consensus model, and 3) demonstrate the FL effectiveness at such scale and task-complexity as a paradigm shift for multi-site collaborations, alleviating the need for data-sharing.

sample_claims.text: The model training process does not require patient data to leave individual healthcare institutions
The keyboard prediction model learns from user typing patterns without transmitting personal text content to central servers
Each participating bank trained the shared fraud-detection model without moving customer transaction records out of its own environment; only model updates reached the coordinator
The central server holds no copy of any participant's raw training data; it holds the shared model and, briefly, the updates it is aggregating

techniques.name: Differential Privacy
techniques.description: Differential privacy puts a mathematical limit on what a published result reveals about any one person. The data holder adds random noise, drawn for example from a Laplace or Gaussian distribution, to each answer before release, such as a count, an average or a table of statistics, so the answer would look almost the same with or without any one person's data. The amount of noise depends on how much one person could change the answer (its sensitivity) and on a privacy budget called epsilon, which sets how far the two cases may differ (the Gaussian mechanism adds a second, small parameter, delta, for the chance of exceeding that limit). A smaller epsilon means more noise, a stronger guarantee and less accurate answers, and each release spends part of the budget. The guarantee covers whether a person's data took part, not conclusions about the wider population that the results legitimately show.

example_use_cases.description: A national statistics office adds calibrated noise to published census tables so that no single household's presence changes the results by more than a set amount. Statisticians use the epsilon setting to decide how much accuracy small areas must give up.

A health authority publishes weekly hospital admission counts by postcode district with Laplace noise added, so a rare diagnosis in a small district cannot be tied to one patient. Its privacy officer sets a yearly budget and decides how many weekly releases it can cover.

An analytics team lets internal analysts query customer purchase data only through an interface that adds noise and tracks each analyst's privacy budget. The data protection lead uses the budget log to decide when an analyst must stop querying.

A model-evaluation team publishes noisy aggregate performance counts for declared groups. It documents the protected unit, sensitivity bound, noise mechanism and cumulative privacy budget so reviewers can interpret the release's guarantee.

limitations.description: Noise lowers accuracy, and for a given epsilon the noise on a count does not shrink as the dataset grows, so small groups, rare categories and fine-grained tables suffer most. A strong guarantee (small epsilon) can make statistics for small subgroups unusable.
Setting the privacy budget (epsilon) requires expertise and careful consideration of the privacy-utility trade-off, with no universal guidelines for appropriate values across different applications.

Each release spends part of a fixed privacy budget, and the epsilons add up across releases. Once the budget is spent, no further analysis of the same data is possible without weakening the guarantee, so releases must be planned in advance.

The guarantee depends on correct sensitivity analysis: if a query's sensitivity is underestimated, or one person can contribute many records, too little noise is added and the stated epsilon no longer holds.

The guarantee concerns whether one person's data took part, not what the results show about the population. Conclusions that hold for everyone still apply to each individual, and protection weakens for groups, such as a family, by a factor equal to the group size.

resources.title: The Algorithmic Foundations of Differential Privacy
resources.abstract: The problem of privacy-preserving data analysis has a long history spanning multiple disciplines. As electronic data about individuals becomes increasingly detailed, and as technology enables ever more powerful collection and curation of these data, the need increases for a robust, meaningful, and mathematically rigorous definition of privacy, together with a computationally rich class of algorithms that satisfy this definition. Differential Privacy is such a definition. After motivating and discussing the meaning of differential privacy, the preponderance of this monograph is devoted to fundamental techniques for achieving differential privacy, and application of these techniques in creative combinations, using the query-release problem as an ongoing example. A key point is that, by rethinking the computational goal, one can often obtain far better results than would be achieved by methodically replacing each step of a non-private computation with a differentially private implementation. Despite some astonishingly powerful computational results, there are still fundamental limitations — not just on what can be achieved with differential privacy but on what can be achieved with any method that protects against a complete breakdown in privacy. Virtually all the algorithms discussed herein maintain differential privacy against adversaries of arbitrary computational power. Certain algorithms are computationally intensive, others are efficient. Computational complexity for the adversary and the algorithm are both discussed. We then turn from fundamentals to applications other than queryrelease, discussing differentially private methods for mechanism design and machine learning. The vast majority of the literature on differentially private algorithms considers a single, static, database that is subject to many analyses. Differential privacy in other models, including distributed databases and computations on data streams is discussed. Finally, we note that this work is meant as a thorough introduction to the problems and techniques of differential privacy, but is not intended to be an exhaustive survey — there is by now a vast amount of work in differential privacy, and we can cover only a small portion of it.

resources.title: Calibrating Noise to Sensitivity in Private Data Analysis
Programming Differential Privacy
The 2020 Census Disclosure Avoidance System TopDown Algorithm
resources.abstract: The Census TopDown Algorithm (TDA) is a disclosure avoidance system using differential privacy for privacy-loss accounting.The algorithm ingests the final, edited version of the 2020 Census data and the final tabulation geographic definitions.The algorithm then creates noisy versions of key queries on the data, referred to as measurements, using zero-Concentrated Differential Privacy.Another key aspect of the TDA are invariants, statistics that the Census Bureau has determined, as matter of policy, to exclude from the privacyloss accounting.The TDA postprocesses the measurements together with the invariants to produce a Microdata Detail File (MDF) that contains one record for each person and one record for each housing unit enumerated in the 2020 Census.The MDF is passed to the 2020 Census tabulation system to produce the 2020 Census Redistricting Data (P.L. 94-171) Summary File.This article describes the mathematics and testing of the TDA for this purpose.

resources.title: RAPPOR
resources.abstract: Randomized Aggregatable Privacy-Preserving Ordinal Response, or RAPPOR, is a technology for crowdsourcing statistics from end-user client software, anonymously, with strong privacy guarantees. In short, RAPPORs allow the forest of client data to be studied, without permitting the possibility of looking at individual trees. By applying randomized response in a novel manner, RAPPOR provides the mechanisms for such collection as well as for efficient, high-utility analysis of the collected data. In particular, RAPPOR permits statistics to be collected on the population of client-side strings with strong privacy guarantees for each client, and without linkability of their reports. This paper describes and motivates RAPPOR, details its differential-privacy and utility guarantees, discusses its practical deployment and properties in the face of different attack models, and, finally, gives results of its application to both synthetic and real-world data.

sample_claims.text: The published census tables were produced by a mechanism satisfying epsilon-differential privacy with a stated epsilon, so adding or removing any one household changes the probability of any published output by at most a factor of e to the power epsilon
Weekly admission counts are released with Laplace noise calibrated to a sensitivity of one patient, and the total privacy budget spent across all releases is tracked and capped
The analytics interface refuses further queries from an analyst once their allocated privacy budget is spent, so cumulative disclosure about any one individual stays within the agreed bound
Aggregate spending statistics shared with a research partner carry a documented epsilon, which bounds how much the partner can learn about whether any one customer's data was included
The model performance metrics across demographic groups are accompanied by documented privacy budget allocation and noise parameters

techniques.name: Homomorphic Encryption
techniques.description: Homomorphic encryption lets a server compute on data that stays encrypted, so the server never sees the underlying values. The data owner encrypts the inputs, the server performs the arithmetic directly on the encrypted data, and only the holder of the secret key can decrypt the result. For machine learning, the model is first rewritten using operations the scheme supports, such as additions, multiplications and polynomial approximations of other functions. Exact schemes return the same answer as the unencrypted computation, while approximate schemes, often used for neural networks, return a close one. The guarantee is confidentiality of the data while it is processed, on the usual assumption that the server follows the protocol.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital group wants a cloud service to score patients' readmission risk without the provider seeing patient records. The hospital encrypts the patient features, the cloud evaluates a logistic regression model on the encrypted values, and the hospital decrypts the scores. A linear model is chosen on purpose, since encrypted computation becomes costly as models get larger.

A bank outsources credit scoring to a third-party cloud host. It encrypts customer financial data under a key that never leaves the bank, so an attacker who breaches the host, or an administrator there, can only copy ciphertexts. The bank checks that the host holds no decryption key and that the chosen parameters meet its required security level.

A research team outsources a genome-wide association study to a cloud server. The team encrypts participants' genotype and phenotype data, the server computes the association statistics on the ciphertexts, and only the final statistics are decrypted. One published prototype handled 1,000 individuals and 131,071 genetic variants in about ten minutes on a 28-core server.

limitations.description: Computation is typically orders of magnitude slower than on unencrypted data and ciphertexts are much larger, so real-time use, large models and large datasets are often out of reach. A published encrypted logistic regression training run took about 116 minutes on a real-world dataset.

Only some computations are practical. Circuit depth is limited by noise growth unless costly bootstrapping resets it, and comparisons and non-polynomial functions, such as most neural-network activations, must be approximated or quantised to integers, which can lower accuracy compared with the unencrypted model.

The usual security model is an honest-but-curious server. Ciphertexts can be altered, so encryption alone gives no assurance that the server ran the intended computation correctly, and a malicious host could return a wrong result that still decrypts without error.

Encryption protects data during processing, not what the result reveals. Whoever decrypts the output can still learn about the model or the data behind it through attacks such as membership inference, and with the approximate CKKS scheme, sharing decrypted results can enable a key-recovery attack.

Correct use needs cryptographic expertise. Choosing scheme parameters, encodings and noise budgets wrongly can leave the system insecure or stop results decrypting correctly, and the right choices differ by scheme and library.

resources.title: Fully homomorphic encryption using ideal lattices
resources.abstract: We propose a fully homomorphic encryption scheme -- i.e., a scheme that allows one to evaluate circuits over encrypted data without being able to decrypt. Our solution comes in three steps. First, we provide a general result -- that, to construct an encryption scheme that permits evaluation of arbitrary circuits, it suffices to construct an encryption scheme that can evaluate (slightly augmented versions of) its own decryption circuit; we call a scheme that can evaluate its (augmented) decryption circuit bootstrappable.

resources.title: Getting started — Concrete ML documentation
Secure Logistic Regression Based on Homomorphic Encryption: Design and Evaluation
resources.abstract: BACKGROUND: Learning a model without accessing raw data has been an intriguing idea to security and machine learning researchers for years. In an ideal setting, we want to encrypt sensitive data to store them on a commercial cloud and run certain analyses without ever decrypting the data to preserve privacy. Homomorphic encryption technique is a promising candidate for secure data outsourcing, but it is a very challenging task to support real-world machine learning tasks. Existing frameworks can only handle simplified cases with low-degree polynomials such as linear means classifier and linear discriminative analysis. OBJECTIVE: The goal of this study is to provide a practical support to the mainstream learning models (eg, logistic regression). METHODS: We adapted a novel homomorphic encryption scheme optimized for real numbers computation. We devised (1) the least squares approximation of the logistic function for accuracy and efficiency (ie, reduce computation cost) and (2) new packing and parallelization techniques. RESULTS: Using real-world datasets, we evaluated the performance of our model and demonstrated its feasibility in speed and memory consumption. For example, it took approximately 116 minutes to obtain the training model from the homomorphically encrypted Edinburgh dataset. In addition, it gives fairly accurate predictions on the testing dataset. CONCLUSIONS: We present the first homomorphically encrypted logistic regression outsourcing model based on the critical observation that the precision loss of classification models is sufficiently small so that the decision plan stays still.

resources.title: Optimized homomorphic encryption solution for secure genome-wide association studies
resources.abstract: Background Genome-Wide Association Studies (GWAS) refer to observational studies of a genome-wide set of genetic variants across many individuals to see if any genetic variants are associated with a certain trait. A typical GWAS analysis of a disease phenotype involves iterative logistic regression of a case/control phenotype on a single-neuclotide polymorphism (SNP) with quantitative covariates. GWAS have been a highly successful approach for identifying genetic-variant associations with many poorly-understood diseases. However, a major limitation of GWAS is the dependence on individual-level genotype/phenotype data and the corresponding privacy concerns. Methods We present a solution for secure GWAS using homomorphic encryption (HE) that keeps all individual data encrypted throughout the association study. Our solution is based on an optimized semi-parallel GWAS compute model, a new Residue-Number-System (RNS) variant of the Cheon-Kim-Kim-Song (CKKS) HE scheme, novel techniques to switch between data encodings, and more than a dozen crypto-engineering optimizations. Results Our prototype can perform the full GWAS computation for 1,000 individuals, 131,071 SNPs, and 3 covariates in about 10 minutes on a modern server computing node (with 28 cores). Our solution for a smaller dataset was awarded co-first place in iDASH’18 Track 2: “Secure Parallel Genome Wide Association Studies using HE”. Conclusions Many of the HE optimizations presented in our paper are general-purpose, and can be used in solving challenging problems with large datasets in other application domains.

Individual-level genotype data stay encrypted at every stage on the analysis server, and only the aggregate association statistics are ever decrypted
A breach of the third-party hosting environment exposes only ciphertexts of the bank's customer data, because the secret key never leaves the bank
Encrypted queries sent to the hosted model reveal neither the client's inputs nor the predictions to the operator, even to an administrator with full access to the server's memory and storage

techniques.name: Conformal Prediction
techniques.description: Conformal prediction wraps any trained model so that, instead of a single answer, it returns a set of plausible answers (an interval, for a numeric prediction) that contains the true outcome at a chosen rate, such as at least 95% of the time. It first scores, on a calibration set of labelled data kept apart from training, how unusual each known outcome looks given the model's prediction, using a nonconformity score, and for a new case it keeps every candidate answer whose score falls below a threshold taken from those calibration scores. A diagnostic model might then return 'cancer or benign tumour' rather than 'likely cancer', and with a suitable score the sets grow larger where the model is less certain. The guarantee is distribution-free, meaning it assumes nothing about the shape of the data, but it does assume the calibration data and new cases are exchangeable, roughly that they come from the same source in no particular order. It holds on average over all cases, not within each subgroup, unless the calibration is done separately within each predefined group (Mondrian conformal prediction), which needs enough calibration cases in every group.

example_use_cases.description: A medicinal chemistry team screening compounds in silico builds prediction sets of the protein targets each compound may be active against, at 95% coverage. Compounds with a single-target set go to lab testing for that target, and those with several targets go to a wider panel, so costly experiments follow how uncertain the model is.

Providing transparent multi-class predictions in judicial risk assessment by showing all plausible risk categories at the stated coverage level, enabling judges to see the full range of possibilities rather than just a single point estimate.

A university predicts whether first-year students will complete their degree and offers early support when the 90% prediction set includes 'withdraws'. To keep that 90% true for every group, not only on average, the data team calibrates the sets separately within each demographic group, then checks coverage and average set size per group on held-out students. A group with too few calibration cases is reported as not covered by the guarantee.

limitations.description: Sets can be wide enough to be useless. A multi-class set holding most classes, or an interval spanning the plausible range, meets the coverage target but tells the decision-maker little, and sets containing opposing outcomes make decisions hard. Width depends on the model's quality and the scoring rule chosen, and the guarantee says nothing about it.

Needs labelled calibration data kept apart from training. On small datasets that means less data to train on, or a coarse and unstable coverage level, and variants that avoid a separate calibration set need several model fits.

The guarantee assumes calibration data and new cases are exchangeable, roughly that they come from the same source in no particular order. Drift, a changed population or strongly time-ordered data break it, and coverage then falls below target with no warning. In Shafer and Vovk's example, a nominal 5% error rate rose to 8% on a systematically different test set.

Coverage is guaranteed on average over all cases, not for each individual or subgroup, so a model can reach 95% overall while covering a minority group far less often. Mondrian calibration fixes this only for predefined, non-overlapping groups. It needs each new case's group at prediction time and is unstable when a group has few calibration cases (MAPIE's tutorial gives under 200 as an example).

Cost depends on the variant. Split conformal prediction adds little beyond scoring a held-out set, but full conformal prediction re-evaluates every candidate outcome and cross-conformal variants refit the model several times, which can be prohibitive for large models or real-time use.
